messages.content:
You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Kioxia In-depth Update: 75% Profit Margin, 800 Billion Yen Buyback, and 155,000 Yen Valuation Anchor

TEXT:
TL;DR
1. J.P. Morgan’s qualitative assessment of this result is only “slightly positive.” Kioxia’s Q1 non-GAAP operating profit was 1.3262 trillion yen, matching company guidance but falling short of market expectations; Q2 revenue guidance is also below market expectations but aligns with J.P. Morgan’s forecast. The report does not shy away from the shortfall, instead emphasizing that continued ramp-up in enterprise SSDs is more important than a single quarter’s weak shipment performance.
2. The explosive profit in Q1 was mainly due to price increases, not volume growth. Revenue reached 1.7671 trillion yen, up 76% QoQ; average selling prices rose about 70% QoQ, bit shipments only grew at a low single-digit percentage, yet non-GAAP operating margin soared to 75%. This proves Kioxia’s strong operating leverage and serves as a reminder: if prices fall, profits may shrink just as quickly.
3. The volume/price mix for Q2 is healthier than Q1, but profitability is still price-driven. The company guides for revenue of 2.39 trillion yen, non-GAAP operating profit of 1.9 trillion yen, and a 79.5% profitability. J.P. Morgan estimates the QoQ revenue growth of 35% may be driven by double-digit bit growth and over 20% increases in average selling prices, with part of the shipments deferred from Q1 making up the rest.
4. Data centers and enterprise SSDs are key for sustaining valuation premiums. SSD and storage revenue came in at 1.1747 trillion yen, 66% of total revenue; data center and enterprise applications account for over 60% of that division. 8th-gen BiCS FLASH output now exceeds 50%, with improvements in both product mix and cost curve, which are more sustainable competitive advantages than a pure NAND price surge.
5. The 800 billion yen buyback boosts per-share value realization, but does not guarantee a price floor. The company authorizes repurchasing up to 30 million shares, about 5.5% of total equity, with an 800 billion yen cap. At the report date’s share price of 46,500 yen, that amount will only buy about 17.2 million shares; the number and amount limits cannot be hit simultaneously at current prices, so average execution price and actual quantity matter more than the theoretical cap.
6. The 155,000 yen target price is maintained, not raised this round. J.P. Morgan continues to use FY2027 earnings per share with an ~11x P/E multiple – about half a standard deviation above the 15-year, 9x industry average. That the target price was not raised after the record results means positive news mostly confirms June’s rerating framework, rather than opening up a new valuation band.
Table of Contents
First look at the report’s tone: Why only “slightly positive”
How did the 75% profit margin come about: price contributed far more than volume
Enterprise SSD improves profit quality, but hasn’t eliminated the cycle
Q2 Guidance: Volume begins to catch up, price still the main engine
800 billion yen buyback: cap announcement is not the same as actual firepower
6. Remaining sections
Record profits haven’t led to unanimous optimism: J.P. Morgan acknowledges Q2 revenue guidance below market expectations but maintains the 155,000 yen target price. The real controversy is, how much of the 75% profit margin can be retained outside of the cycle.
First look at the report’s tone: Why only “slightly positive”
If you only look at YoY growth, this is an earnings report that can easily distort your sense of scale. Kioxia’s Q1 revenue was up 415% YoY, non-GAAP operating profit up 2833% YoY—one-quarter’s operating profit at 1.3262 trillion yen already exceeds the entire FY2025 total of 876.2 billion yen. Normally such figures would point to a “significantly above expectation” report, but J.P. Morgan characterizes it as just “slightly positive.”
The reason is that sell-side research compares results to expectations, not just YoY growth. Q1 operating profit met company guidance but fell below market expectations; Q2 revenue guidance is below market, but matches J.P. Morgan’s model. To put it simply: The company earned a lot, but the market was expecting even more.
This also explains the seemingly exaggerated gap between the share price on the report date and the target price. J.P. Morgan lists the July 31 share price as 46,500 yen, with the target price still at 155,000 yen, which appears to be roughly 3.33x higher. Such a wide gap does not mean that one quarter’s profit has created over twice as much new value; rather, the stock has already fallen sharply from prior highs and the market has started discounting peak-cycle earnings more heavily.
This article needs to answer two questions: How much of the 75% profit margin comes from sustainable product and cost advantages? Why is the market unwilling to simply annualize the Q2 79.5% margin?
How did the 75% profit margin come about: price contributed far more than volume
